newsitem.title: UK: EU grain prices sustained by subsidy, export hopes.
newsitem.headline: EU grain prices sustained by subsidy, export hopes.

text.p: Expectations of further European Union subsidised sales and good export demand helped sustain grain prices in major European markets this week, traders said.

The EU last week reverted to granting subsidies to its main grain exporters for the first time in more than a year after a bumper harvest in several areas. Subsidies had been suspended in early 1995 when world supply tightened.

UK's Home-Grown Cereals Authority said even if EU grain exports were to rise by 50 percent above last year's 20 million tonnes, latest EU crop estimates suggest EU intervention stocks would still rise bymore than 10 million tonnes this season.
"Hence, the EU grain prices are expected to be closer to support levels this season than has been the case over the past two years," it said in its weekly bulletin.

Traders in France said wheat prices were steady this week underpinned by hopes the EU would continue to encourage exports of subsidised wheat and help cover a large sale of 450,000 tonnes of French wheat to Egypt.
French wheat into Rouen for Oct/Dec delivery was broadly unchanged from the 890-895 francs per tonne level it reached last Friday on the subsidy news.
This week's focus was on barley following trade reports Saudi Arabia bought about 1.4 million tonnes of barley for import between October and December.
The purchase, which has yet to be confirmed, was made at prices ranging from $146-$158 per tonne C and F.
The EU is widely expected to help cover a large part of the contract with tonnages split between intervention and free-market stocks.
France, facing prospects of a bumper barley crop, hopes to benefit from the sale as it plans to export 1.8 million tonnes of barley to non-EU destinations in the new season.
In Germany, wheat export prices remain at high nominal levels as buyers look to other EU countries for fourth quarter purchases and sellers are absent, brokers said.
Farmers were storing and assessing the harvest and saw no need to get involved in marketing discussions, and traders were busy carrying out recent business, they added.
"EU millers are covered for the next few weeks and hope for price falls later on in 1996 amid supply pressure," one said.
"Sellers are refusing to give in to this argument because of eastern European demand for wheat, barley and rye."
Brokers also said harvest delays meant quality assessments were still patchy and this blurred the price scenario for the near future.
UK grain prices were slightly steadier this week on good export demand but gains were limited by harvest pressure.
Latest estimates show that UK's wheat crop harvest could be closer to 16 million tonnes than 15 million and up sharply from 14.31 million in the last season.
In Spain, rain continued to delay maize harvests in the north, but the outlook for the crop remains good, traders said. The harvest is now expected from the second week of October.
In Italy, wheat prices were stable to lower this week as the new harvest fills the market which does not have enough demand to absorb it, dealers said.
"There are reliable forecasts that Italy's 1996 durum wheat harvest will come in at some 3.7 million tonnes, but I think these estimates are lower than the actual harvest," one said.
"The quality of the harvest was not particularly good so many millers started refurbishing from abroad," one dealer said.

The dealer noted that in those areas, mainly in the north, where it was easy to bring in foreign wheat prices this week had dropped, while in the central regions prices were unchanged at higher levels.
"Producers in central Italy had to buy also Italian soft wheat because transportation problems delayed the arrival of the foreign crop," the dealer added.
Maize prices are still very volatile as the harvest is trying to get underway but has been delayed by the bad weather.
